# hostdiary data — guide for AI readers

hostdiary is a resource diary for ONE Linux host: minute-by-minute measurements,
daily summaries and browser graphs in the HotSaNIC style. This directory is its
public output, collected from procfs. AI-first means JSON and this guide for an
external AI, not an embedded AI or API call. It records measurements, OOM kills,
observed application starts, gaps, directory changes (by comparing daily lists)
and estimated boots. It does not record reasons, service health or logs. hostdiary
applies no thresholds, makes no normal/abnormal judgement and sends no alerts:
deciding what matters is the reader's job.

## Read in this order

1. `index.json` — host name, `generated_at` (time of the last collection, Unix
   seconds), `boots` (estimated boot times), `unavailable` (sources that could
   not be read in the last collection) and `groups`. Each group has `columns`,
   `units` and English `descriptions`, `last_seen`, the UTC `days` with minute
   files, and coarse files. Network groups also have a monthly traffic estimate.
2. `summary.json` — for every retained UTC day and group: `rows`, `first`,
   `last`, `missing_minutes`, `gaps`, and per column `count`, `min`/`min_time`,
   `max`/`max_time`, `mean` (and `sum` for `mem.oom_kills` and `app.started`).
   Start a health check here instead of scanning every minute file.
3. `data/1m/<UTC-date>/<group>.jsonl` — one-minute rows for the newest eight
   UTC days. Open these to look at a specific time range found in step 2.
4. `data/5m/<UTC-month>/`, `data/1h/<UTC-month>/`, `data/1d/<UTC-year>/` —
   coarse values for longer periods (the newest 3 month files, 25 month files,
   and three year files respectively).
5. `data/dirs/<UTC-date>.json` — the newest 31 daily directory usage lists, when enabled.

Minute data and its summaries cover the newest eight UTC day directories (more
while rollup is failing). Past boots cover the last 1095 days (about 3 years),
including the cutoff; the current boot is kept even when older. Daily values use
three year files, so their retained period is not the same as the boot window.

Files ending in `.js` mirror the JSON for the offline browser view; ignore them.

## Questions and where to look

| Question | Where to look |
|---|---|
| When did this host reboot? | `index.json` → `boots`: estimated recorded boots, limited by retention, missing observations and state loss. |
| What happened last night? | Convert the local window to UTC. Use retained `summary.json` days/groups, then matching `data/1m` files. If minute files are gone, use indexed coarse files. |
| How does this compare with last week? | Compare matching windows in retained minute or coarse files, checking units, samples and nulls. For directory changes compare the same path in retained dirs files; absence is not zero. |
| Why did it happen? | Reasons, service health and logs are not recorded. Use these numbers as evidence, then consult external logs. |

## JSONL format

A line starting with `{` is a header: `columns` and `units` apply to the array
lines that follow, until the next header. A line starting with `[` is a row:
`[time, value, ...]`. Match values to columns by position under the header that
precedes them, never by a fixed column order. Skip lines that are not valid JSON.

Coarse rows are `[time, samples, last_time, c1, c1_max, c2, c2_max, ...]`:
`time` is the START of the interval, `c` is the mean and `c_max` the maximum of
the minute values in it, `samples` the number of minute rows.
The browser shows coarse OOM kills as a mean and a maximum, not a total. For AI
calculations, `oom_kills`/`started` mean times samples is only an approximate
interval total: samples is not the per-column non-null count, and means are
rounded to three decimals. A positive OOM maximum indicates kills even when
the mean rounds to zero.

## Rules that are easy to get wrong

- Days are UTC. Convert to local time only for display.
- No row means no data for that minute (collection stopped, skipped or failed).
  It does not mean zero. `missing_minutes` and `gaps` in summary.json count
  minute slots without a row.
- `null` means "could not be read or calculated". It is not zero. Rates are
  null on the first collection after a boot or after a gap longer than 180 s.
- Units ending in `/s` are PER SECOND. A row holds the average rate since the
  previous valid collection (normally about 60 s earlier; null when that
  interval is over 180 s). Multiply by 60 for an approximate count per minute.
  summary.json keeps the original units and never rescales them.
- `count` columns are mostly states at the moment of collection (processes,
  connections, inodes). Only `mem.oom_kills` and `app.started` count events
  since the previous collection; their daily total is `sum` in summary.json.
- Maxima of different columns can come from different minutes: never add
  maxima together (for example CPU columns, or used_max + avail_max).
- `mem.oom_kills` includes kills caused by cgroup memory limits; compare it with
  `mem.available` before concluding the host ran out of memory.
- `net.rx_drops` also counts frames without a protocol handler; it is not
  end-to-end packet loss. `tcp.retrans_segs / tcp.out_segs` is a retransmission
  ratio, not a packet loss rate.
- RSS sums per application count shared memory again for every process.
- A day with `"status": "partial"` in summary.json is today and still growing;
  compare its `expected_minutes` (minutes elapsed so far) with `rows`.
  `"future"` means the host clock was ahead when the day was written.
- `"complete"` only means a past UTC day; it does not guarantee a day without
  gaps or nulls. Check missing_minutes and per-column count. An absent day, group or column
  is not zero: it may be outside retention, unreadable or not collected.
- `boots` lists boots that hostdiary observed. A boot missing from the list is
  not proof that the host did not reboot. The last entry is the last recorded
  boot, not necessarily the current boot: if boot identity or uptime could not
  be read after a reboot, an earlier boot can remain last for up to 1095 days.
  Losing, corrupting or being unable to read private state.json loses this
  history; only the current observation restarts it. Expired history cannot be
  recovered by extending retention. Same-boot estimates remain fixed.
- An old `generated_at` may mean collection stopped or that you are reading an
  old copy. Check the source's freshness before drawing a conclusion. A group
  whose `last_seen` is older than `generated_at` has no newer recorded row;
  it may have disappeared or failed collection. This is not a service-health check.

## Suggested health check

1. Check `generated_at` in index.json and the freshness of the source or copy.
   Do not conclude that collection stopped solely from an old copied index.
2. In summary.json, look at `missing_minutes` per day and group.
3. Look for non-zero `max` in error and event columns: `oom_kills`,
   `rx_errors`, `rx_drops`, `tx_errors`, `tx_drops`.
4. Compare `min` of `mem.available`, `max` of `psi` columns, `max` of
   `diskio.busy` and the latest `disk.avail` with earlier days; use `min_time`
   and `max_time` to open the matching minute file for details.
5. Report numbers with their units and UTC/local times, and say which values
   were null or missing.

The full format specification is docs/data-format.md in the hostdiary source.
